description: We are building Ares, an AI-powered mission intelligence platform for human exploration of Mars. Our goal is to integrate NASA scientific datasets into an interactive Martian map, analyze terrain and hazards, optimize astronaut routes, and simulate mission constraints such as oxygen, energy, and time. We welcome passionate developers, AI/ML engineers, data scientists, and designers interested in space exploration, scientific computing, and solving real-world engineering challenges.
summary:
ARES (Mars Mission Planning and Terrain Intelligence System) is an interactive decision-support prototype designed to support preliminary Mars rover route assessment around Jezero Crater. It combines real Mars elevation data from the USGS MOLA–HRSC blended Digital Elevation Model with a derived terrain-slope map to help users understand variations in surface steepness.
The dashboard allows users to select science objectives, configure mission constraints such as maximum travel time, oxygen margin, and allowable slope, and adjust priorities including science value, safety, time, and energy efficiency. ARES then evaluates and ranks illustrative route scenarios using deterministic scoring, helping users compare mission trade-offs.
By making terrain information and planning constraints easier to explore, ARES demonstrates how geospatial data and interactive decision-support tools can contribute to more informed Mars mission planning. It is a research prototype, not an autonomous navigation system; its route scenarios are illustrative rather than validated rover traverses.
details:
ARES (Mars Mission Planning and Terrain Intelligence System) is an interactive web-based decision-support prototype for preliminary rover route assessment around Jezero Crater on Mars.

How it works: ARES processes real Mars elevation data from the USGS MOLA–HRSC Blended DEM (200 m resolution) to derive terrain slopes and display them as a classified map. Users can explore terrain information, select science objectives, configure mission constraints including maximum travel duration, minimum oxygen margin, and maximum allowable slop and adjust priorities such as science value, safety, time, and energy efficiency. A deterministic scoring system evaluates and ranks three illustrative route scenarios, allowing users to compare mission trade-offs and understand how changing priorities affects route selection.

Benefits and intended impact: ARES brings terrain intelligence and mission-planning considerations into one interactive interface. It demonstrates how geospatial analysis and configurable decision-support systems can help mission planners explore potential trade-offs, identify terrain concerns, and make more informed preliminary assessments.

Technology: The project uses React, TypeScript, and Vite for the frontend, Python and FastAPI for the backend, and Rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, and PyProj for geospatial processing and terrain analysis. The processed slope raster and terrain summary are served through API endpoints and integrated into the dashboard.

Creativity and design considerations: ARES combines planetary terrain visualization with configurable mission constraints and multi-criteria route ranking. Our team considered terrain steepness, scientific objectives, mission duration, oxygen reserves, safety, energy efficiency, and usability when designing the prototype. We also aimed to make the system transparent by distinguishing measured terrain information from illustrative route scenarios.

ARES is a decision-support prototype rather than an autonomous navigation system; its route scenarios are illustrative and are not validated rover traverses.
